_about: Call versions of the seed scenarios (same codes as email.json). Each call is a script in three parts read by text-to-speech: the opening, the hook (which always offers 'press 1' or 'say yes'), and a pressure line played once if the person stays quiet. Taking the hook, or staying on through the pressure line, switches to a different voice that says it was a Safekeep practice, names the warning signs, and offers a text with the coaching link. Pressing 9 at any point stops practice calls. The build sets each scenario's content to the three parts joined, so the warning signs quote what was said.

scenarios.name: Parcel redelivery fee

script.opening: Hello. This is an automated message from the parcel delivery service. We tried to deliver your package today, but there is an unpaid redelivery fee of one dollar and ninety-nine cents.
script.hook: To pay the fee now and schedule your delivery, press 1 or say yes.
script.pressure: If the fee is not paid today, your package will be returned to the sender. Press 1 now to keep your delivery.

tells.quote: an unpaid redelivery fee
tells.note: Delivery companies don't phone you to collect a fee for trying again.

tells.quote: This is an automated message from the parcel delivery service
tells.note: No company name and no tracking number, so it could be about anyone's parcel.

tells.quote: If the fee is not paid today
tells.note: The deadline is there to hurry you.

next_steps: I'll hang up and check the tracking on the shop's own website.
I won't give a card number to a recorded call.
If I'm not expecting a parcel, I'll ignore it.
scenarios.learning_objective: Delivery companies don't call to collect fees.
scenarios.debrief: Recorded delivery calls work for the same reason the texts do: most people have something on the way. The small fee is the door to your card number.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A recorded call asking you to pay a redelivery fee
The call coming in the daytime
question.affirm: That's right. A delivery company won't call asking for a fee.
question.gently: Understandable, but the clearest sign is the fee itself. A delivery company won't call to collect one.

scenarios.name: Sweepstakes win with a fee

script.opening: Congratulations! This is the Prize Notification Center. Your phone number was selected as a grand prize winner of eight hundred and fifty thousand dollars.
script.hook: To claim your prize, press 1 or say yes, and an agent will explain the small processing fee.
script.pressure: This offer expires at the end of today. Please do not tell anyone until your winnings are released. Press 1 now.

tells.quote: Your phone number was selected
tells.note: You can't win a contest you never entered.

tells.quote: the small processing fee
tells.note: Paying to receive a prize is the scam, every time it comes up.

tells.quote: Please do not tell anyone
tells.note: Secrecy keeps you from talking to someone who'd spot it at once.

next_steps: If I didn't enter, I didn't win, so I'll hang up.
I won't pay anything to collect a prize.
I'll tell someone in the family about calls like this.
scenarios.learning_objective: Paying a fee to collect a prize is the prize scam.
scenarios.debrief: Prize calls are built on hope. Whatever the amount, they come down to one request: send a little money to receive a lot.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Winning something you never entered, with a fee to collect
question.affirm: Yes. A contest you didn't enter and a fee to collect give it away.
question.gently: The big number is eye-catching, but the clearest sign is winning something you never entered and paying to collect it.

scenarios.name: Virus warning call

script.opening: This is the Computer Security Center calling about your computer. Our system has detected five viruses, and your personal files and banking information may be at risk.
script.hook: To speak with a certified technician who can remove them now, press 1 or say yes.
script.pressure: Please do not turn off your computer, as this may cause permanent data loss. A technician is standing by. Press 1.

tells.quote: Our system has detected five viruses
tells.note: Nobody can see viruses on your computer from the outside and call you about them.

tells.quote: Please do not turn off your computer
tells.note: Turning it off is safe. This line keeps you anxious and on the phone.

tells.quote: a certified technician
tells.note: The 'technician' asks to connect to your computer, then for payment or your bank login.

next_steps: I'll hang up on anyone who calls about my computer out of the blue.
If I'm worried, I'll ask someone I know or a shop I choose.
I won't let a caller connect to my computer.
scenarios.learning_objective: Unsolicited calls about viruses are tech support scams.
scenarios.debrief: Tech support scams start with a scare and end with someone connected to your computer. Real companies don't call you about viruses.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A caller claiming they can see viruses on your computer
Being asked to keep the computer on
question.affirm: That's it. Nobody can see your computer from the outside.
question.gently: That line is designed to scare you. The first sign is the claim itself: nobody can see your computer from outside.

scenarios.name: Bank account locked

script.opening: This is the account security team at your bank. We noticed unusual sign-in activity and have locked your account for your protection.
script.hook: To unlock it now, press 1 or say yes, and have your card number and PIN ready.
script.pressure: If you do not verify within the next hour, your account will be closed. Press 1 to verify now.

tells.quote: the account security team at your bank
tells.note: It never says which bank. Your real bank would.

tells.quote: your card number and PIN
tells.note: No bank ever asks for your PIN.

tells.quote: your account will be closed
tells.note: Banks don't close accounts because you didn't answer a call.

next_steps: I'll hang up and call the number on the back of my card.
I'll never give my PIN to anyone who calls.
I'll check my account the way I always do.
scenarios.learning_objective: Your bank never asks for your PIN on the phone.
scenarios.debrief: Account-locked calls make your money feel in danger and offer a quick fix. Hanging up and calling the number on your card tells you the truth in a minute.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being asked for your card number and PIN
A call from a security team
question.affirm: Yes. A bank will never ask for your PIN.
question.gently: Banks do mention unusual activity, which is why this works. The giveaway is the request for your PIN.

scenarios.name: Power shut-off today

script.opening: This is the utility billing department with a final disconnection notice. Your electric service is scheduled to be shut off today at four o'clock for a past-due balance.
script.hook: To avoid disconnection, press 1 or say yes to pay now by prepaid gift card.
script.pressure: Do not contact your local office, as they cannot stop the disconnection. Only this line can help. Press 1 now.

tells.quote: scheduled to be shut off today at four o'clock
tells.note: Utilities send written notices for weeks before any shut-off.

tells.quote: prepaid gift card
tells.note: No utility takes gift cards.

tells.quote: Do not contact your local office
tells.note: Being told not to check is the clearest sign of all.

next_steps: I'll hang up and call the number on my last paper bill.
I'll never pay a bill with a gift card.
I'll ask someone if I'm unsure.
scenarios.learning_objective: Same-day shut-off threats and gift cards are utility scam signs.
scenarios.debrief: Utility scams use the fear of losing power. A real utility gives written notice and takes ordinary payments, and is happy for you to call them.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being told not to contact your local office
question.affirm: Right. A real company never tells you not to check with them.
question.gently: The time is meant to rush you. The surest sign is being told not to contact your local office.

script.hook: To resolve this today by paying the fine, press 1 or say yes to speak with an officer.

tells.note: Courts don't threaten arrest on the phone.

tells.quote: officers may be sent to your address
tells.note: The threat is there to frighten you into paying.

I won't pay a fine over the phone to someone who called me.
I'll tell family, since these count on embarrassment.
scenarios.learning_objective: Courts don't threaten arrest or collect fines by phone.
scenarios.debrief: Jury duty scams rely on worry and embarrassment. A quick call to the court clerk, on a number you found, puts it to rest.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A caller offering to cancel a warrant if you pay a fine
question.affirm: Yes. Courts don't take a payment over the phone to cancel a warrant.
question.gently: Official words are part of the disguise. The sign is the offer to make a warrant go away if you pay.

scenarios.name: "It's me" on the phone

script.opening: Hi, it's me. Please don't be upset. I'm in some trouble and I lost my phone, so I'm calling from a friend's. I really need help paying something today.
script.hook: Can you help me? Press 1 or say yes and my friend will tell you where to send the money.
script.pressure: Please don't tell Mom or Dad yet, I'll explain everything later. I really need you right now. Press 1.

tells.quote: Hi, it's me
tells.note: Someone you know would say their name. 'It's me' lets you fill in who you think it is.

tells.quote: I lost my phone, so I'm calling from a friend's
tells.note: This stops you from calling them back on their own number, which is exactly what to do.

tells.quote: Please don't tell Mom or Dad yet
tells.note: Secrecy keeps you from finding out they're fine.

next_steps: I'll hang up and call them on the number I already have.
If I can't reach them, I'll call someone else in the family.
We'll agree a family code word for emergencies.
scenarios.learning_objective: "It's me" calls asking for urgent, secret money are family emergency scams.
scenarios.debrief: This is the grandparent scam, and voices can now be faked with AI, so the voice itself is not proof. Calling the number you already have settles it.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: No name, a borrowed phone, and a request to keep it secret
The call coming in the day
question.affirm: Exactly. Those three together are how these keep you from checking.
question.gently: Sounding upset is part of the act. The clearest sign is no name, a borrowed phone and the secrecy.

scenarios.name: Disaster relief appeal

script.opening: Hello, I'm calling for the Storm Relief Fund. Thousands of families lost their homes this week, and tonight every gift is doubled by a generous donor, but only until midnight.
script.hook: Can we count on you for fifty dollars tonight? Press 1 or say yes.
script.pressure: Gifts by gift card or wire transfer reach families fastest. The match ends at midnight. Press 1 to give now.

tells.quote: only until midnight
tells.note: Real charities welcome gifts any time. A countdown stops you looking them up.

tells.quote: Gifts by gift card or wire transfer
tells.note: Established charities don't ask for gift cards or wires.

tells.quote: Storm Relief Fund
tells.note: A name that sounds right but you've never heard of is worth looking up first.

next_steps: I'll give to charities I already know, on their own websites.
I won't give over the phone to a charity that called me.
I won't give by gift card or wire.
scenarios.learning_objective: Fake charities use deadlines and untraceable payments.
scenarios.debrief: Fake charity calls appear after every disaster. Giving through a charity you know, on its own website, gets your money to the right place.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Asking for a gift card or wire transfer
question.affirm: Yes. Real charities don't ask for gift cards or wires.
question.gently: Real news makes it convincing. The clearest sign is the payment method.

scenarios.name: Medicare plan ending

script.opening: Hello, this is the Medicare benefits office calling during Open Enrollment. Your current plan has been flagged for changes that could leave you without coverage on January first.
script.hook: To review your coverage now with a benefits advisor, press 1 or say yes. Please have your Medicare number ready.

tells.quote: Please have your Medicare number ready
tells.note: Medicare doesn't call to ask for your number. It's used to bill for things you never got.

tells.quote: for the next forty-eight hours
tells.note: Open Enrollment lasts for weeks. Nobody official gives you 48 hours.

tells.quote: this is the Medicare benefits office calling
tells.note: Medicare doesn't make calls like this. If something needed checking, you'd get a letter.

next_steps: I'll hang up and call the number on my Medicare card.
I won't give my Medicare number to anyone who calls me.
I'll review plans with someone I trust, like a SHIP counselor.
scenarios.learning_objective: Medicare doesn't call asking for your Medicare number.
scenarios.debrief: This one arrives during real Open Enrollment, when you're expecting news about your plan, which makes it harder. The short deadline and the request for your number give it away.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A caller asking for your Medicare number with a 48-hour deadline
question.affirm: That's right. That combination is the one to watch for.
question.gently: The timing makes it believable. The giveaway is the deadline and the request for your number.

scenarios.name: Tax refund waiting

script.opening: This is the tax refund department. After a review of your recent filing, you are eligible for an additional refund of twelve hundred and eighty-four dollars.
script.hook: To receive it by direct deposit, press 1 or say yes, and an agent will confirm your bank details and Social Security number.
script.pressure: Refunds not claimed within five business days are returned to the Treasury. Press 1 now.

tells.quote: you are eligible for an additional refund
tells.note: The tax agency contacts people by post, not by phone, about refunds.

tells.quote: your bank details and Social Security number
tells.note: Those two together let someone take over your accounts.

tells.quote: within five business days
tells.note: A refund you're owed doesn't vanish because you didn't answer quickly.

I'll never give my Social Security number to someone who called me.
I'll ask someone I trust if I'm unsure.
scenarios.learning_objective: The tax agency doesn't call about refunds or ask for your Social Security number.
scenarios.debrief: Good news lowers people's guard, which is why refund calls work. The request for your bank and Social Security details is what to notice.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being asked for bank details and your Social Security number on a call

question.gently: The exact amount is there to seem real. The clearest sign is the request for your bank and Social Security details.

scenarios.name: Surprise renewal charge

script.opening: Hello, this is billing support. Your annual device protection plan renewed today for three hundred ninety-nine dollars and ninety-nine cents.

tells.quote: to speak with a refund agent

tells.quote: within twenty-four hours
tells.note: The rush stops you checking your real statement.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?

scenarios.name: Friendly stranger calling

script.opening: Oh, hello. I'm so sorry, I think I've dialled the wrong number. I was trying to reach an old friend from my years in the service. You have such a kind voice, though.

tells.quote: I'm working overseas

I won't share my details with someone I don't know.
I'll never send money to someone I haven't met in person.
scenarios.learning_objective: "Wrong number" openers from lonely, overseas strangers are how romance scams begin.
scenarios.debrief: Romance scams start slowly and kindly. The opening is the easiest place to spot them, because it follows a familiar pattern.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A stranger calling by mistake, sharing a loss, and working overseas

question.gently: Politeness is part of the charm. The pattern to notice is the wrong number, the shared loss and the job overseas.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: A caller asking for part of your Social Security number

question.gently: The timing makes it feel real. The clearest sign is the request for your Social Security number.

script.pressure: For your safety, keep this confidential, including from family members. It is part of an active investigation. Press 1 now.

tells.quote: an agent who will help secure your funds
tells.note: Government agencies never call to help move your money.

tells.quote: keep this confidential, including from family members
tells.note: Secrecy from family is the biggest warning sign of all.

tells.quote: your computer was accessed by an overseas group
tells.note: A frightening claim you can't check is how this scam starts.

next_steps: I'll tell someone in the family straight away, whatever I've been asked.
I won't move money because of a call, even from someone who says they're from the government.
I'll call my bank on the number on my card.
scenarios.learning_objective: The 'phantom hacker' scam chains a tech scare, a fake bank and a fake agent.
scenarios.debrief: This is a version of what the FBI calls the phantom hacker scam. Each step makes the next one more believable. Telling family breaks the chain.

question.prompt: If this had been real, what would have been the first sign it wasn't?
choices: Being told to keep it from family and let an agent secure your money
question.affirm: Yes. Secrecy from family and an agent for your money give it away.
question.gently: The scary details rush you. The clearest signs are the secrecy and the agent for your money.
